subject: maths
title: Chapter 2 · Test 4
summary: Chapter 2 test 4: parallel lines, triangle angle sums, quadrilateral properties, and interior and exterior angles of polygons.
body: This test covers Chapter 2: angles and parallel lines, angle sums of triangles, properties of quadrilaterals, interior angles of polygons and exterior angles. It has 15 questions, from easy to challenge. Allow about 25 minutes. Work with no notes and no calculator unless the question says. Diagrams are drawn to scale, but always use the angle rules and the facts you are given — never measure. Write your working, give a reason for each step, and check that your answer is the angle the question asks for (not just the value of x).

questions.prompt: AB ∥ CD and ∠PQC = 131°. Find x, the size of ∠BPQ, in the diagram.
questions.explanation: x and 131° are between the parallel lines on opposite sides of the transversal (a Z shape), so they are alternate angles and x = 131. 49 treats them as co-interior.
steps: Both angles are between AB and CD, on opposite sides of PQ — alternate angles (Z shape).
Alternate angles on parallel lines are equal.

mistakes.A: Step 2: alternate angles are equal — do not subtract from 180°.
mistakes.B: Step 2: there is no right angle here; alternate angles are simply equal.
mistakes.C: Step 2: alternate angles are equal — do not double the angle.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel lines AB and CD cut by a transversal at P and Q. Angle BPQ (right of the transversal, below AB) is x and angle PQC (left of the transversal, above CD) is 131°

questions.explanation: The angles of a triangle add to 180°, so x = 180 − 58 − 77 = 45. 135 stops after adding the two known angles.
steps: The angles of a triangle add to 180°.

mistakes.B: Step 2: 135 is the two known angles added. Subtract this from 180.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the angles of a triangle add to 180°, not 360°.
mistakes.D: Step 2: subtract BOTH known angles from 180, not just 58.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle ABC with angle A = 58°, angle B = 77° and the angle at C marked x

questions.prompt: The diagram shows a regular octagon. Find the size of each interior angle.
questions.explanation: An octagon's angles add to (8 − 2) × 180 = 1080°, and the 8 angles are equal, so each is 1080 ÷ 8 = 135°. 45° is the exterior angle.
steps: A regular octagon has 8 equal angles.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 45° is the exterior angle (360 ÷ 8). The interior angle is 180° minus it.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 1080° is the sum of all 8 angles. Divide by 8.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the angle sum uses n − 2 = 6 triangles, not n − 1 = 7.

questions.diagram_alt: A regular octagon with all sides equal; one interior angle is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: Side AB of the polygon is extended past B. The interior angle at B is 98°. Find the exterior angle x.
questions.explanation: The interior and exterior angles at B lie on a straight line, so x = 180 − 98 = 82°. 262° wrongly uses 360°.
steps: The interior angle and the exterior angle at B sit on the straight line through A and B.
Angles on a straight line add to 180°.

mistakes.A: Step 2: interior and exterior angles add to 180° (a straight line), not 360°.
mistakes.D: Step 1: x is the exterior angle, next to the 98° angle on the straight line — it is not equal to it.

questions.diagram_alt: Pentagon ABCDE with side AB extended past B (dashed). The interior angle at B is 98° and the exterior angle at B is marked x

questions.prompt: AB ∥ CD and the line bends at E, as shown. ∠ABE = x°, ∠CDE = 48° and ∠BED = 2x°. Find ∠BED.
questions.explanation: The tip angle equals the sum of the arm angles: 2x = x + 48, so x = 48 and ∠BED = 96°. 48 is only x.
steps: Subtract x from both sides: x = 48.

mistakes.B: Step 2: 48 is the value of x. The question asks for ∠BED = 2x.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the tip angle equals the SUM of the arm angles: x + 48 = 2x.
mistakes.D: Step 1: ∠CDE and ∠BED are not on a straight line. Use the arrowhead rule: tip = sum of arms.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel lines AB and CD with a line bending at E between them, like an arrowhead pointing right. Angle ABE is x°, angle CDE is 48° and angle BED is 2x°

questions.prompt: In triangle ABC, AB = AC. Side CA is extended past A to E, and ∠BAE = 104°. Find ∠ABC.
questions.explanation: The exterior angle ∠BAE equals the sum of the interior opposite angles ∠ABC + ∠ACB. These are equal base angles, so each is 104 ÷ 2 = 52°. 76° is the apex angle ∠BAC.
steps: ∠BAE is an exterior angle of triangle ABC, so it equals ∠ABC + ∠ACB.
AB = AC, so ∠ABC = ∠ACB — the two base angles are equal.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 76° is ∠BAC (180 − 104), the apex angle. Find the base angles next.
mistakes.C: Step 2: the base angles share 180 − 76 = 104°, so each is 52°. Halving 76 halves the wrong angle.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 104° is the exterior angle, equal to BOTH base angles added together. Halve it.

questions.diagram_alt: Isosceles triangle ABC with AB and AC marked equal. Side CA is extended past A to E; angle BAE is 104°. Angle ABC is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: ABCD is a kite with AB = AD and CB = CD. ∠BAD = 80°, ∠BCD = 60°, and ∠ABC = ∠ADC = (2x + 10)°. Find x.
questions.explanation: The angles add to 360°, so the two equal angles share 360 − 140 = 220°, each 110°. Then 2x + 10 = 110 gives x = 50. 110 is the angle, not x.
steps: The angles of a quadrilateral add to 360°, so the two equal angles together are 360 − 80 − 60 = 220°.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 110° is the size of each equal angle (2x + 10). Now solve 2x + 10 = 110.
mistakes.B: Step 1: there are TWO angles of (2x + 10)°. Write 80 + 60 + 2(2x + 10) = 360.
mistakes.D: Step 3: subtract the 10 first: 2x + 10 = 110 gives 2x = 100. Do not just halve 110.

questions.diagram_alt: Kite ABCD with AB = AD (one dash) and CB = CD (two dashes). Angle BAD is 80°, angle BCD is 60°, and angles ABC and ADC are each (2x + 10)°

questions.prompt: The pentagon in the diagram has three right angles and two equal angles of x°. Find x.
questions.explanation: A pentagon's angles add to 540°. The three right angles use 270°, so 2x = 270 and x = 135. 270 forgets to share between the two equal angles.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 45 would be the exterior angle. x is the interior angle.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 270 is the two x angles together. Divide by 2.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the angle sum of a pentagon is 540°, not 450°; x is not another right angle.

questions.diagram_alt: A house-shaped pentagon ABCDE with right angles at A, B and D, and angles of x° at C and E

questions.prompt: The diagram shows one exterior angle at each corner of a triangle: 140°, 95° and x. Find x.
questions.explanation: The exterior angles of any convex polygon, including a triangle, add to 360°, so x = 360 − 140 − 95 = 125°. 55° is the interior angle at that corner.
steps: One exterior angle at each corner: they add to 360°.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 55° is the interior angle at that corner. x is the exterior angle.
mistakes.C: Step 2: subtract BOTH known exterior angles from 360°, not just 95°.
mistakes.D: Step 3: 40° is the interior angle next to the 140° exterior angle, not x.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle ABC with each side extended. The exterior angles are 140° at A, 95° at B and x at C

questions.prompt: AB ∥ CD. P is on AB, and Q and R are on CD. ∠APQ = 70° and ∠BPR = 45°. Find ∠QPR.
questions.explanation: ∠APQ, ∠QPR and ∠BPR sit side by side on the straight line AB, so ∠QPR = 180 − 70 − 45 = 65°. (Or: ∠PQR = 70° and ∠PRQ = 45° by alternate angles, then use triangle PQR.) 115° stops after adding.
steps: At P, the angles ∠APQ, ∠QPR and ∠BPR make up the straight line AB.
Angles on a straight line add to 180°.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 115° is 70 + 45. The three angles at P on line AB add to 180°, so subtract.
mistakes.B: Step 2: ∠QPR is not 70 − 45. The three angles at P on the straight line AB add to 180°.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 110° is 180 − 70, which still includes the 45° angle. Subtract both.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel lines AB and CD. From P on AB, lines go down to Q and R on CD. Angle APQ is 70°, angle BPR is 45°, and angle QPR is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: In the diagram, side BC is extended to D. ∠A = (x + 30)°, ∠B = (2x − 10)° and the exterior angle ∠ACD = (5x − 40)°. Find ∠ACB.
questions.explanation: Exterior angle = sum of interior opposite angles: 5x − 40 = 3x + 20, so x = 30 and ∠ACD = 110°. ∠ACB = 180 − 110 = 70°. 110° is the exterior angle.
steps: Exterior angle = sum of the two interior opposite angles: 5x − 40 = (x + 30) + (2x − 10) = 3x + 20.
Subtract 3x and add 40 to both sides: 2x = 60, so x = 30 and ∠ACD = 5 × 30 − 40 = 110°.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 110° is the exterior angle ∠ACD. ∠ACB is the interior angle next to it.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 30 is the value of x, not an angle in the triangle.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 60° is ∠A (x + 30). The question asks for the angle at C inside the triangle.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle ABC with side BC extended past C to D. Angle A is (x + 30)°, angle B is (2x − 10)°, the exterior angle ACD is (5x − 40)°, and angle ACB is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: ABCD is an isosceles trapezium with AB ∥ DC and AD = BC. ∠DAB = 70° and the diagonal AC makes ∠CAB = 30°. Find ∠ACB.
questions.explanation: In an isosceles trapezium the base angles are equal, so ∠ABC = ∠DAB = 70°. In triangle ABC, ∠ACB = 180 − 30 − 70 = 80°. 30° is ∠ACD, a different angle at C.
steps: AD = BC, so the base angles at A and B are equal: ∠ABC = ∠DAB = 70°.

mistakes.B: Step 3: 30° is ∠ACD (alternate to ∠CAB). ∠ACB is the angle between CA and CB.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 110° is ∠BCD. In an isosceles trapezium ∠ABC equals ∠DAB = 70°; use triangle ABC.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 180 − 70 − 70 = 40 uses the wrong triangle. In triangle ABC the angle at A is 30°, not 70°.

questions.diagram_alt: Isosceles trapezium ABCD with AB parallel to DC and AD = BC, and diagonal AC. Angle DAB is 70°, angle CAB is 30°, and angle ACB is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: ABCDEF is a regular hexagon. The diagonals AC and AD are drawn. Find ∠ACD.
questions.explanation: Each interior angle is 120°. Triangle ABC is isosceles (AB = BC) with ∠ABC = 120°, so ∠BCA = 30°. Then ∠ACD = ∠BCD − ∠BCA = 120 − 30 = 90°. 120° is the whole corner angle.
steps: Each interior angle of a regular hexagon is 720 ÷ 6 = 120°, so ∠ABC = ∠BCD = 120°.
AB = BC, so triangle ABC is isosceles: ∠BCA = (180 − 120) ÷ 2 = 30°.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 120° is the whole interior angle ∠BCD. Diagonal CA cuts off ∠BCA = 30°.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 30° is ∠BCA, the part of the angle at C inside triangle ABC.

questions.diagram_alt: Regular hexagon ABCDEF with all sides marked equal and dashed diagonals AC and AD. Angle ACD is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: A regular polygon has n sides and another has 2n sides. Each exterior angle of the first is 15° bigger than each exterior angle of the second. Find n.
questions.explanation: Exterior angles are 360/n and 360/(2n) = 180/n. Their difference is 180/n = 15, so n = 12. (Check: 30° − 15° = 15° ✓.) 24 is the other polygon.
steps: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon = 360 ÷ number of sides: 360/n and 360/(2n).

mistakes.A: Step 3: 24 is 2n, the number of sides of the second polygon. The question asks for n.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 15° is the difference between the exterior angles, not the number of sides.

questions.prompt: AB ∥ CD. The line from B bends at E and goes to D, as shown. ∠ABE = 130° and ∠CDE = 140°, where A and C are on the left. Find ∠BED.
questions.explanation: Draw a line EF through E, parallel to AB, pointing left. Co-interior angles give ∠BEF = 180 − 130 = 50° and ∠FED = 180 − 140 = 40°, so ∠BED = 50 + 40 = 90°. Equivalently the three angles add to 360°. 270° wrongly uses the arrowhead "add" rule.
steps: Draw a line through E parallel to AB and CD, pointing left (back towards A and C).
Co-interior angles: the top part of the angle at E is 180 − 130 = 50°, and the bottom part is 180 − 140 = 40°.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the "tip = sum of arms" rule only works when the arm angles are measured on the side the bend points to. Here they are on the other side.
mistakes.C: Step 3: (360 − 270) ÷ 2 halves the answer for no reason. The angle at E is the whole of 360 − 270.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 270 ÷ 2 is not a rule. Draw a line through E parallel to AB and use co-interior angles.
